Intel’s Tiny Bridges Could Lead to Very Big Paychecksby Daniel Nenni on 11-01-2026 at 12:00 pm

View Profile

View Forum Posts

View Articles

Private Message

Categories: 3D IC, Chiplet, Intel Foundry, Semiconductor1 Comment

Key takeaways ▼

Intel’s next big opportunity could come from something that sounds spectacularly unglamorous: connecting tiny pieces of silicon. Advanced packaging rarely attracts the attention lavished on powerful processors or artificial intelligence models. Yet it increasingly determines how effectively those technologies perform. For Intel, making separate chips behave like one tightly integrated system could become a valuable business of its own.
The logic starts with a practical problem. AI systems need enormous computing power, fast memory and efficient communication between components. Building everything into one gigantic chip becomes increasingly difficult and expensive. Instead, designers can divide a processor into smaller chiplets, manufacture different pieces using suitable technologies, then connect them inside a single package. The connections become central to the finished product’s capabilities.
This is where Intel’s alphabet soup gets interesting. EMIB, short for Embedded Multi-die Interconnect Bridge, uses small silicon bridges embedded in a package substrate to connect neighboring chips. Rather than placing a large silicon connection layer beneath the entire assembly, Intel concentrates dense connections where they are needed. The company argues that this approach offers advantages in cost, flexibility and scaling.
Foveros adds another dimension by allowing chiplets to be stacked vertically. Think of EMIB as connecting buildings across a neighborhood and Foveros as adding floors. Together, these technologies give designers more ways to combine computing, memory and other functions. Intel’s newer EMIB-T technology also introduces connections through its bridges, improving power delivery and supporting the bandwidth requirements of increasingly ambitious systems.
The commercial attraction extends beyond Intel’s own processors. Its packaging services can integrate chiplets produced using different manufacturing technologies and foundries. A customer could therefore use Intel to assemble a sophisticated product without committing every component to Intel’s wafer factories. That creates a potentially useful entry point: customers can purchase a specific capability while keeping flexibility elsewhere in their supply chains.
That distinction matters for Intel’s wider manufacturing ambitions. Winning an entire processor manufacturing contract requires customers to make consequential technical and commercial commitments. Packaging offers another way to begin working together. Intel itself has described customers approaching first for advanced packaging, with successful execution helping build confidence in its broader foundry services. The opportunity is both immediate business and a foundation for deeper relationships.
The billions in the headline represent potential, rather than established packaging revenue. Growing demand for complex AI systems creates an opening for suppliers that can integrate more components reliably and economically. Intel’s technical roadmap targets substantially larger assemblies, including configurations accommodating at least sixteen high-bandwidth memory stacks by 2028. Those plans illustrate the scale of the systems it hopes to serve; they remain forward-looking development targets.
Intel has also given the effort organizational weight. In June 2026, it appointed semiconductor veteran Seok-Hee Lee to lead advanced packaging, system integration and related manufacturing activities. Establishing dedicated leadership signals that packaging is becoming a focused business priority, with execution and customer delivery receiving attention alongside the underlying engineering. The appointment supports the strategy, although leadership changes alone cannot guarantee commercial success.
There are substantial hurdles. Complex packages must meet demanding standards for manufacturing yield, heat management, testing and reliability. Customers need confidence that Intel can deliver consistently at production scale. Revenue will depend on actual design wins, volumes and pricing, while profits will also reflect investment and operating costs. Technical promise, however impressive, must translate into products that customers can ship economically.
Bottom line: Intel does not need to design every winning AI chip to benefit from AI infrastructure spending. It can supply the intricate connections that help other companies’ designs work. If those capabilities earn sustained customer trust, this deeply nerdy manufacturing specialty could become a meaningful growth engine, turning microscopic bridges into a much larger commercial opportunity.
